slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 1/4
bullets: Specimen: Sputum (at least 3 specimens 8–24 hours apart, one early in the morning)

What it is used for: AFB tests are mainly used to diagnose active TB, especially after a positive TB screening test, an abnormal chest x-ray or symptoms; in people on treatment they show whether it is working and whether the person is still infectious. Symptoms of lung TB include a cough lasting three weeks or more, coughing up blood or sputum, chest pain, fever, night sweats and unexplained weight loss.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 2/4
bullets: Physiology: Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) are bacteria that cause tuberculosis and other mycobacterial infections such as leprosy. There are four tests: smear microscopy (results in 1–2 days but cannot diagnose); culture (confirms the diagnosis, but per MedlinePlus takes 6–8 weeks); a molecular test (NAAT — detects TB bacteria directly in sputum in under two hours and can check rifampicin resistance); and drug susceptibility testing.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 3/4
bullets: Per CDC, an optimal bacteriologic examination has five parts: specimen collection, transport and processing; AFB smear classification; direct detection of M. tuberculosis by nucleic acid amplification (with molecular detection of resistance where applicable); culture and identification; and drug susceptibility testing. Smears are stained and examined for AFB, with results due within 24 hours of collection. AFB seen are counted and graded 1+, 2+, 3+ or 4+ — the higher the grade, the more infectious the patient.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 4/4
bullets: WHO recommends rapid diagnostic tests — molecular assays and biomarker-based point-of-care tests — as the initial test for everyone with signs and symptoms of TB; they give initial results within 48 hours of sample collection.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: Positive result: A positive smear means TB or another mycobacterial infection is likely, but culture is needed to confirm: microscopy cannot tell M. tuberculosis from non-tuberculous mycobacteria. Because culture takes weeks, treatment may be started in the meantime. A positive NAAT means TB is probable.

Positive result: Culture is the gold standard for laboratory confirmation: growth of M. tuberculosis confirms TB disease. Drug susceptibility testing is done on the first positive culture; with risk factors for drug resistance or a positive smear or NAA result, specimens go immediately for molecular resistance testing.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Negative result: Negative smears do not exclude TB, and a negative culture does not necessarily rule it out — some patients are diagnosed on clinical grounds. A negative result can also mean there were not enough bacteria in the sample.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: At least three consecutive sputum specimens are examined, collected 8–24 hours apart with at least one early in the morning. Collect them in an airborne infection isolation room, a sputum booth or another isolated, well-ventilated area. Other methods include sputum induction, bronchoscopy and gastric washing.

Sputum is thick mucus coughed up from the lungs, not saliva. Breathe deeply, cough and spit into a sterile container. If not enough comes up, breathing a sterile saline mist can help; if that fails, bronchoscopy is done. Smear and culture are usually done at the same time.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Sputum is usually collected in the morning, and you may be asked to rinse your mouth with water first. The sample is thick sputum coughed up from the lungs, not saliva; the textbooks treat saliva or watery samples as unsuitable.

Limitations: NAA and Xpert MTB/RIF results guide treatment and isolation decisions but do not replace AFB smear, culture, growth-based drug susceptibility testing and genotyping. All specimens should be cultured regardless of the smear result.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: A positive TB blood test (IGRA) or skin test usually means TB infection but does not show active disease — chest x-ray and bacteriology are needed. Some people with TB disease test negative on these. When TB is the presumptive diagnosis, especially in a very ill patient, treatment is not delayed while waiting for bacteriology.

slides.title: Rules for collecting sputum and macroscopic signs
bullets: Before collecting sputum the teeth are cleaned and the mouth rinsed; sputum is collected in the morning, fasting, into a sterile container; 3–5 mL is enough for testing.
The analysis should be done within 2 hours of collection; before delivery to the laboratory the closed container is kept in a refrigerator.
A healthy person normally produces no sputum; it is a pathological secretion of the airways brought up by coughing.

slides.title: Rules for collecting sputum and macroscopic signs
bullets: Bloody sputum is seen in pulmonary infarction, tumours and lung injury; rusty colour reflects breakdown of erythrocytes, in lobar pneumonia.
Raspberry-coloured sputum can occur in tumour autolysis or other malignant lung growths; a foul or putrid smell of fresh sputum occurs when tumour cells break down or in lung gangrene.
Drugs (for example rifampicin) can also change the colour of sputum.

slides.title: Sputum cytology: atypical cells and elastic fibres
bullets: Malignant tumour cells are uncommon in sputum: they are found mainly when the tumour grows into the bronchus and breaks down.
In chronic bronchial inflammation, metaplastic epithelium takes on atypical features and differs little from tumour cells.
So tumour cells are accepted only when atypical clusters and polymorphic cells are seen, especially on a fibrous background or together with elastic fibres.

slides.title: Sputum cytology: atypical cells and elastic fibres
bullets: More than 25 squamous epithelial cells per field means the material is mixed with saliva.

Elastic fibres appear when lung tissue breaks down: tuberculosis, abscess, echinococcosis, lung tumours; Curschmann spirals — in obstructive bronchial disease (bronchial asthma, obstructive bronchitis, lung tumours).
Many leukocytes indicate marked inflammation; eosinophils point to bronchial asthma and helminth involvement of the lungs.

slides.title: Per CDC, how is sputum collected when pulmonary TB is suspected?
options: One specimen at any time is enough
At least three specimens 8–24 hours apart, one early in the morning
A saliva sample in a shared ward
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: At least 3 consecutive specimens 8–24 hours apart, at least one early morning, in an isolated well-ventilated area.

slides.title: No AFB are seen on the sputum smear, but clinical suspicion is high. Correct conclusion?
options: TB is ruled out; no culture needed
Just repeat the smear in a month
TB is not excluded: culture the specimen and consider NAA
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. Culture is the gold standard and is done regardless of the smear.

Basis: Negative smears do not exclude TB; all specimens are cultured.

slides.title: By which method can Helicobacter pylori be detected:
Cytodiagnosis of tumors of the respiratory organs?
bullets: 1. Material: sputum (morning, several days), bronchial wash and brushing, bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial and EBUS-TBNA aspirates, pleural fluid.
2. Squamous cell carcinoma: keratinized, with dense orange cytoplasm (Pap), pleomorphic cells, hyperchromatic pyknotic nuclei; immunophenotype p40+.

3. Adenocarcinoma: groups and glandular/papillary structures, vacuolated cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli; TTF-1 and Napsin-A positive; preserve material for molecular tests (EGFR, ALK, etc.).

slides.title: Cytodiagnosis of tumors of the respiratory organs?
bullets: 4. Small cell carcinoma: small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclei "molded" to each other, fine chromatin, crush artifact; neuroendocrine markers.
5. Sensitivity depends on the material and tumor location: for central tumors sputum and washings are more effective, for peripheral ones – guided aspiration; EBUS-TBNA in diagnosis and staging.
6. Differentiation from reactive changes (metaplasia, regeneration, viruses).
